coach_says: Your bishop on f2 is attacked by the rook on f1 and your king is on the same file, so Rf3+ was already a threat: check, the king moves, and the rook takes f2. Kf5 keeps your king on the f-file, so Rf3+ still skewers king and bishop and you lose the bishop. Step off the file with Ke6, Kg6 or Ke5 and the bishop stays safe.
concept: king left on the skewer file

coach_says: Your d6 pawn is under pressure from e5, and right now White's own queen on d5 blocks the d-file. Offering the queen trade with Qc6 removes that block: after Qxc6 bxc6 exd6 your bishop is attacked and you can't take back on d6 because the rook on d1 now sees it, and c5 drops too. Before trading queens, check what the trade opens up; Qe8 keeps the queens on and lets you meet exd6 with Bxd6.

The d5 pawn was only protected by White's queen, and Qxd5 takes it safely: if White trades queens your knight on f6 recaptures, and you go two pawns up in a calm endgame. Bd6 develops but leaves your extra e4 pawn loose, and White wins it back with Nc3 and Nxe4. When you are already a pawn up, grab free material that also trades queens.

You are already a pawn down, and c5 puts another pawn on a square nothing defends: Black's f8 bishop just takes it with Bxc5, developing at the same time. Pawn pushes in the opening should gain something; this one gives away a pawn and doesn't develop a piece. Bd3 protects e4 and gets you closer to castling.

White's queen on f5 was threatening Qh7+ Kf8 Qh8 mate, because h7 and h8 have no defenders once the knight and h-pawn are gone. Bxb2 grabs a pawn and ignores this, and White mates in two. Every move, ask what your opponent wants to do next; here g6 (kicking the queen) or Qf6 (covering h8) stops the mate.

Your knight on e5 is attacked twice, by the knight on f3 and the bishop on b2, and it was defended twice, by the bishop on d6 and the queen on e7. Taking back with the queen pulls one defender away, so Nxe5 just wins the knight. Recapture with the king (Kxd7): it looks odd, but it keeps the queen guarding e5. Before you recapture, count attackers and defenders on your other pieces.

White's knight on f3 attacks your e5 pawn, and Bc5 does nothing to protect it, so Nxe5 wins a pawn. You can win it back with Qe7, but only by moving your queen early and losing time. Protect e5 first with Nc6 (or d6), then bring the bishop to c5 next move.
also: respond to the opponent's threat first

coach_says: Your bishop had to move because of hxg4, but taking on f3 hands White a free developing move: the queen lands on f3 and eyes b7 and h5, and with your king still in the centre and your kingside pawns broken, Qh5+ and d4 come fast. That light-squared bishop was the piece defending the squares around your king. Keep it with Bh5, which keeps the pin and covers those light squares.

Rf4 attacks the bishop, but it just steps back to g3, where it now hits c7, and your rook has to move again. Meanwhile your bishop on c8 and rook on a8 are still at home, so Re8+ trades off your active rook and c7 falls. Attacking a piece is only useful if it has nowhere good to go; here finish your development first with b6 or c5 and then the bishop and rook.
concept: chasing a piece to a better square

coach_says: Your queen had to move and keep guarding c2 against Nxc2+, and Qf2 does that, but on f2 it can be hit again by Ng4 and has to move a second time. Qd3 also guards c2 and attacks the d4 knight, and no black piece can kick it there. When you move your queen out of danger, pick a square where it won't be chased with tempo.
also: guard c2 from the knight fork

coach_says: Black's queen on f6 already points at f2, and Bc5 would add a second attacker on a square only your king defends. Bb5 pins a knight to nothing and doesn't help f2 at all, so after Bc5 your position falls apart. Nc3 develops and, after Bc5, Nxe4 attacks the queen and bishop and blocks the attack on f2. Before a developing move, check which of your squares the opponent is aiming at.

Black's queen has grabbed a pawn on b3 and is stuck deep in your camp with very few squares. The right idea is to keep it locked in and then hunt it: a5 or Rfb1 leaves it short of exits and you win the queen or a lot of material. Na5 attacks it but moves your knight away and lets the queen out to c3, where it can trade itself off. When an enemy queen is short of squares, take away its exits before you attack it.
Nf6 is a sensible developing move that hits e4, as good as anything here. The real problem was the move before: Bxf2+ gave up a bishop for a pawn. From here just develop and castle.
Bd8 saves the attacked bishop and is about as good as the alternatives; you are a pawn down after the earlier queen trade either way. Keep an eye on stopping the d-pawn.
c5 is a perfectly good reply to 1.Nc3 and leads to normal Sicilian-type positions. Nothing to fix here.
Rc1 is the best practical try: it takes the open file and eyes c7. You are worse after the earlier trades, but this move was fine.
g5 is fine; you stay clearly better with the d7 pawn tying Black down. Rd1 to support the passed pawn was a touch more direct, but the difference is small.
The position is lost whatever you play, as the f7 pawn is about to promote, and Ne5 is as good a try as any. Nothing here to learn from this move.

Black's king is stuck on e8 with the e8-h5 diagonal wide open, and the bishop on f5 is the only piece guarding it. Nd4 attacks that bishop, and if exd4 then Qh5+ checks and wins the bishop on f5. Castling is a fine move but gives Black time to fix the problem. When the enemy king is exposed, look for checks with your queen and for ways to attack its defenders.
also: Qh5+ fork on the e8-h5 diagonal

coach_says: When f6 attacked your bishop, retreating with Bf4 let Black play fxe5 dxe5 and free their position. Taking first with exf6 (or Bxf6) trades off Black's g7 bishop, the main defender of their dark squares, and after Bxf6 Bxf6 Rxf6 the knight on f5 is the only thing between your queen and the rook on f6, so g4 wins material. When a pawn attacks your piece, check whether an exchange gains more than a retreat.
also: g4 hits the f5 knight shielding the rook
